lesenParts.text: Last summer, I decided to do something completely different. Instead of spending my holidays at home, I signed up for a volunteer program in a small village in the Peruvian Andes. I had always wanted to travel, but I wanted to do more than just visit tourist sites; I wanted to make a real difference. When I arrived, I was surprised by how different everything was. The air was thin, the mountains were breathtaking, and the local community was incredibly welcoming. My main job was to help build a new classroom for the primary school. I had never held a hammer or painted a wall before, but the local builders were very patient with me. They taught me how to mix cement and how to work as part of a team. It was hard physical work, especially in the heat, but I felt a great sense of achievement every evening. In the afternoons, I helped the children with their English homework. They were so eager to learn, and we often spent hours laughing as we tried to communicate through gestures and simple words. Living without electricity and limited internet access was a challenge at first. I missed my friends and the comforts of home, but as the weeks passed, I realised that I didn't need those things to be happy. I learned to appreciate the simple things, like a shared meal or a beautiful sunset over the peaks. This experience changed my perspective on life. I realised that we don't need much to be happy, and that helping others is one of the most rewarding things you can do. I returned home with a new sense of purpose and a promise to myself that I would continue volunteering in the future. I have already started looking for local opportunities in my own city.

Modern cities are undergoing a significant transformation as urban planners prioritize the creation of green spaces. For many years, concrete and glass dominated the skyline, but now the focus is shifting towards parks and gardens. (1) ________. These areas act as the lungs of the city, filtering pollutants and providing a necessary escape from the noise of traffic. 

Research has shown that access to nature significantly improves the mental health of residents. (2) ________. Consequently, city councils are investing millions into converting unused industrial land into public parks. Some of these projects are quite ambitious, involving the planting of thousands of native trees and the creation of artificial lakes. (3) ________. 

However, maintaining these spaces requires careful planning and constant funding. It is not enough to simply plant grass and trees; the city must ensure that these areas remain safe and accessible for everyone. (4) ________. This includes installing proper lighting and creating well-maintained paths for walkers and cyclists. 

Ultimately, the goal is to create a sustainable urban environment where people and nature can coexist. (5) ________. By making cities greener, we are not only improving our quality of life today but also ensuring a healthier future for the next generation.

lesenParts.text: Organising a surprise party for a friend can be a lot of fun, but it requires careful planning. First, you need to decide on a date and time that work for everyone. It is essential to keep the plan a secret, so make sure you do not tell the person (1) ______ birthday it is! You might want to create a group chat online, but be careful (2) ______ you add to it. Ask everyone to arrive at the venue at least thirty minutes before the guest of honour. This ensures that everyone is hidden (3) ______ the person arrives. You should also think about the food and drinks. A buffet is usually the best option (4) ______ it allows people to move around and talk to each other easily. Don't forget to decorate the room with balloons and banners to make it look special. Finally, when the person walks in, remember to shout 'Surprise!' as loudly as you can. It is a moment (5) ______ they will definitely remember for a long time. If you follow these simple steps, your surprise party (6) ______ be a huge success.

horenParts.transcript: Hello everyone. I am here to tell you about the exciting changes coming to our local library next month. First, we are introducing a new online reservation system. You will be able to book books from home using your library card number. We are also opening a new study area on the second floor, which will be equipped with ten high-speed computers. For those who enjoy reading outside, we are launching a 'Books in the Park' scheme where you can borrow items from a mobile stand near the fountain. Please note that the library will be closed for renovations on the 15th of July. If you need help with your digital skills, we are starting free weekly workshops every Wednesday morning. Finally, if you have any suggestions, please leave a note in the suggestion box located next to the main entrance.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who designs video games for a living. Sarah, was it always your dream to work in this industry? Sarah: Actually, no. I studied architecture at university. I loved drawing buildings, but I found the work a bit slow. One day, a friend showed me how to code a simple game, and I was hooked. I realised that game design is like architecture, but you can build entire worlds that people can interact with. Interviewer: That sounds fascinating. What is the most challenging part of your job? Sarah: People think it is just playing games all day, but it is actually very stressful. We have strict deadlines. If the game isn't ready for the holiday season, the company loses a lot of money. Sometimes I spend 12 hours a day staring at code. Interviewer: Do you ever get tired of it? Sarah: Sometimes, but then I see someone playing a game I helped create, and their face lights up. That feeling is worth all the hard work. Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people wanting to enter the field? Sarah: Don't just play games—learn how they are made. Start with simple tools and don't be afraid to make mistakes. Your first game will probably be terrible, and that is perfectly fine!

questions.question: What does Sarah think about making mistakes?
questions.explanation: She says it is perfectly fine to make mistakes when starting out.
options: a) It means you are not talented
b) It is a normal part of learning
c) It should be avoided at all costs

questions.question: What did Sarah originally study at university?
questions.explanation: Sarah mentions she studied architecture at university before getting into game design.
options: a) Game design
b) Computer science
c) Architecture

questions.question: What does Sarah say is the most difficult part of her job?
questions.explanation: She explains that the work is stressful due to strict deadlines.
options: a) Playing games all day
b) Working with other designers
c) Meeting strict deadlines

questions.question: How does Sarah feel when she sees people playing her games?
questions.explanation: She says the feeling of seeing people enjoy her work makes the hard work worth it.
options: a) She feels surprised
b) She feels it is worth the effort
c) She feels she should have done better

questions.question: What is Sarah's advice for young designers?
questions.explanation: She suggests learning how games are made rather than just playing them.
options: a) Play as many games as possible
b) Study architecture first
c) Learn how games are created

questions.question: Why did Sarah change her career path?
questions.explanation: She found architecture work to be too slow and became interested in coding games.
options: a) She found architecture too slow
b) She failed her architecture exams
c) She wanted to earn more money

schreibenParts.task: Read this email from your friend Sam and the notes you have made. Write an email to Sam answering all your notes. (100 words). Email: 'Hi! I'm so excited about our weekend trip next month! I was thinking we could go to the mountains. What do you think? Also, should we travel by train or bus? I'm planning to bring my camera, but what else do you think I should pack? Let me know if you have any other ideas for activities!' Notes: 1. Say you love the mountain idea. 2. Choose train (faster). 3. Suggest packing a warm jacket. 4. Suggest visiting the local lake.
